title: F1 Live to return in 2027 with unmissable Milan fan event
excerpt:
Formula 1 is set to light up Milan as it brings an incredible three-day entertainment spectacle to the Italian city from February 18-20 2027, known as F1 Live Milan.

Born from an ambition to create an event for fans that was even bigger and more immersive than F1 75 Live at the O2 in 2025, which was streamed across 37 global territories and drew 7.5 million viewers to the live broadcast, F1 Live Milan will offer two distinct opportunities for fans: Milan Fan Festival, which will run across all three days; and F1 The Show, a high-octane, one night-only spectacle with appearances from the drivers and Team Principals of all 11 teams, as well as music, entertainment, and more.

The event will transform an iconic city venue into the ultimate high-energy F1 destination. The expanded three-day format reflects F1’s commitment to placing fans at the heart of the sport, and will combine the atmosphere of fan festivals in race cities around the world with more opportunities than ever to be immersed in the world of F1 and its future.

F1 The Show will take place for one night only on February 18 2027, bringing together the stars of F1, along with an exciting entertainment and music line-up for an unforgettable spectacle that captures the spirit of the sport.

London, where F1 75 Live took place, will hand the baton to Milan, Italy – a city and country with a deep and enduring passion for the sport. As a global capital of culture, creativity, and design, and just a short distance from Monza, the legendary home of the Italian Grand Prix and one of F1’s most historic venues, Milan offers the perfect stage for the return of F1 Live.

F1 Live Milan will take place just ahead of the start of the 2027 F1 season, where the teams and drivers are set to deliver even closer wheel-to-wheel racing and fantastic drama both on and off the track.

Further exciting details about F1 Live Milan, including activity across each day of the Milan Fan Festival and the line-up for F1 The Show, will be revealed in the coming months. Tickets will go on sale later this year, and fans will also be able to pre-register their interest. Those unable to join the action in Milan will still be able to experience F1 Live Milan across a broad range of channels.

Stefano Domenicali, President & CEO of Formula 1, said: “We are always thinking big and pushing boundaries, and F1 Live Milan is going to be an incredible experience created with our fans at its heart. We want them to feel that they are not simply watching the sport, but they are truly immersed in it.

“It is an important part of our ongoing ambition to bring Formula 1 closer to fans than ever before, giving them the chance to see their heroes up close and experience the energy, innovation, and emotion that make Formula 1 so unique.

“As F1 continues to reach new audiences around the world, racing will always be our soul – but we also want to create unforgettable experiences that bring the excitement of Formula 1 to life on an even bigger scale and continue to explore what is possible.

“Building on the extraordinary success of F1 75 in London, F1 Live Milan will transform the city into a Formula 1 festival for three unforgettable days, bringing people together from across the globe to celebrate everything they love about our sport.

“I know my fellow Italians will offer a fantastic welcome to fans travelling to F1 Live Milan and I cannot wait to see the city come to life with Formula 1 energy, creating memories that will last a lifetime.”

title: Leclerc leads Hamilton in first Italian GP practice
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc set the pace during first practice at the Italian Grand Prix, the Monegasque leading a Ferrari 1-2 from team mate Lewis Hamilton while Mercedes’ George Russell was third.

At the stage of the session where many were switching to the soft tyres for their flying runs, Leclerc went fastest of all on the medium compound with his effort of 1m 23.008s – a time that stood until the end of the hour.

The opening practice session in Monza featured a few different names on the timesheets, with four rookies participating. Ayumu Iwasa was driving Max Verstappen’s Red Bull, while Williams’ Alex Albon had made way for Luke Browning, Paul Aron returned in Pierre Gasly’s Alpine and Colton Herta was getting his third run of the season in place of Cadillac’s Sergio Perez.

Meanwhile Liam Lawson was embarking on his second consecutive weekend for Red Bull, with the New Zealander continuing to stand in for an injured Isack Hadjar – meaning that Yuki Tsunoda had also been given another opportunity in Lawson’s seat at Racing Bulls.

Iwasa led out a queue of cars in hot and sunny conditions as FP1 got underway at 1230 local time, the majority of the pack sporting hard tyres for their early laps while some opted for the medium or soft compound.

With the track busy from the off, traffic proved to be an issue for some – including the rookies, with Iwasa complaining about Aron after encountering the Alpine ahead of him on the racing line. Meanwhile Russell had set the fastest time during the first quarter of the session, the Mercedes driver recording a lap of 1m 23.802s to go nearly four tenths clear of Lando Norris.

Shortly afterwards the yellow flags were thrown when Herta came to a halt out on track with a suspected hydraulic issue, the American having been asked by the team to stop the car. A Virtual Safety Car was subsequently called before the session was red-flagged as the marshals worked to clear the MAC-26.

With just over half of FP1 left when the action resumed, Norris was leading the timesheets on a 1m 23.719s as the drivers returned to the track. Some had switched to the soft tyres for their first flying laps, including the Mercedes pair of Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

While this initially put Russell at the top, Leclerc soon bettered the Briton's effort on the medium tyres with a lap of 1m 23.008s – undoubtedly giving the watching Tifosi something to cheer about.

This time put the Monegasque three tenths ahead of Russell, with Hamilton in third and Antonelli – sporting a special Valentino Rossi-inspired helmet for his home race – holding fourth. Aron, meanwhile, had again sparked the ire of another driver as Tsunoda took to the radio to complain about the Estonian being in his path.

As the final quarter of the session played out, the track remained busy as the teams and drivers set about completing their programmes. Hamilton was amongst those to improve and moved up to P2, less than two tenths behind his team mate.

Leclerc’s earlier benchmark ultimately proved unbeatable, the Monegasque leading a Ferrari 1-2 while Russell was three tenths adrift of the top spot in third. Lawson claimed fourth in the Red Bull, followed by Antonelli and Norris while Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, Franco Colapinto in the Alpine and Aron completed the top 10.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri placed in 11th, ahead of Tsunoda and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg, with Ollie Bearman – in an upgraded Haas – claiming P14. Browning was 15th followed by the other Williams of Carlos Sainz, while Iwasa, Fernando Alonso in the Aston Martin, Haas’ Esteban Ocon, Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas and the other Aston Martin of Lance Stroll were next.

Herta, meanwhile, rounded out the classification after only completing five laps before his stoppage on track.

The drivers and teams will now have a chance to reconvene and examine their data before Free Practice 2 takes place at 1600 local time.

title: Rosso Corsa: Why Ferrari race in red – and when they haven’t
excerpt:
As the story goes, Enzo Ferrari once said, “Ask a child to draw a car, and he will certainly colour it red.” Scuderia Ferrari and ‘Rosso Corsa’ scarlet is one of the most iconic colour combinations in motorsport – but where did this partnership begin? Ahead of the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, and with Ferrari running a special Schumacher-inspired livery at the Temple of Speed, let’s take a trip down memory lane.

Ferrari are the most successful team in Formula 1 history, with a record 16 Constructors’ Championships to their name, and have always been associated with vibrant red liveries.

This weekend the team are running a special livery to commemorate Michael Schumacher’s 1996 victory in Monza, complete with seven stars on the front nose to mark the legend’s seven Drivers’ Championships.

Why are Ferraris red?

Before teams could customise their liveries to the extent we see today, cars were colour-coded based on nationality. These standardised colours made it clear where a team or driver was from, and some of these allocated colours have stuck around on modern machines.

Italy was red, and that colour was shared amongst Ferrari and other Italian manufacturers – like Alfa Romeo and Maserati – in the early seasons of the Formula 1 World Championship. France was blue like Alpine run today, Great Britain was green as you see on the current Aston Martin machines, and Germany was white.

All these colour connections date back as early as the 1900s, but for the 1968 season rules were relaxed on running sponsorship across the cars, which changed the commercial side of the sport forever.

Enzo Ferrari, the founder of Ferrari, was a very passionate Italian and wanted to showcase this by running his cars in the mandated national colour. The very first machine to come from their Maranello base – the Ferrari 125 S which debuted in May 1947 – was in racing red.

Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for home Grand Prix at Monza

What is Rosso Corsa?

Rosso Corsa is a beautiful shade of red some fans instantly think of when imagining Ferrari. It’s the shade that the team will be running this weekend, and almost has a retro feel to it.

Literally translated as ‘Racing Red’, the colour was designed to look quick and show off the lines of the car by being flat and not using any metallic flakes.

However, the team now typically uses a lighter shade titled 'Rosso Scuderia', which was created to have a more visual pop on television screens.

There have also been darker shades of red used by Ferrari in F1, including their 1000th Grand Prix livery which embraced burgundy and paid tribute to a similar shade seen on Ferrari's cars in the 1950 Monaco Grand Prix.

Have Ferrari ever not raced in red?

It’s a common question, and the answer is yes. Although Ferrari have added pops of colour to their liveries – like yellow seen at the 2022 Italian Grand Prix or blue at the 2024 Miami Grand Prix – the last time the works team ran a fully non-red car was in 1964.

When Ferrari raced in blue

The story goes that Enzo Ferrari ordered the blue-and-white paint job for the final two races of the 1964 season in protest, after the governing body at the time refused to homologate his new machine for the World Sportscar Championship that season.

Losing the iconic trademark red was a huge shock among the paddock, with the blue and white inspired by the North American Racing Team, who were the group behind importing Ferraris into the United States.

When Ferrari raced in yellow

Privateer cars have also been branded in yellow in the past, with perhaps the best example being Olivier Gendebien at the 1961 Belgian Grand Prix at Spa-Francorchamps. The Belgian driver was behind the wheel of a factory Ferrari 156 with its famous ‘sharknose’ design, but was a private entry and ran in yellow – the national racing colour of Belgium.

Gendebien finished in fourth, and saw Ferrari secure a historic 1-2-3-4 result – the last time any constructor achieved this in F1.

When Ferrari raced in green

Finally, and not used across a Formula 1 World Championship event, Ferrari-badged cars have raced in British Racing green thanks to Vanwall.

The team previously raced modified Ferraris in Formula Libre races, and whilst Ferrari supplied plenty of key components, the car was mainly modified and assembled by the Vanwall squad.

title: Why Ocon isn't receiving the new Haas power unit in Monza
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix is a big weekend for Haas as the team brings its first major upgrade package since Canada back in May.

The VF-26 has slipped towards the tail of the midfield pack in recent races, having been jumped by Aston Martin’s AMR26. There’s also been a rollercoaster of form between Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon, with typically one struggling and the other a lot happier on a given weekend.

For Monza there’s also an extra boost for Bearman, who gets the sole example of the latest Ferrari power unit – upgraded through the ADUO process – that has been allocated to customer team Haas.

“We are very much hoping that we have a bit more performance this weekend,” Bearman said on Thursday. “It’s been a good few races now that we’ve kind of been left behind by our competition. It’s been a while that we’ve brought a big upgrade to the car, and so we have a lot of hopes set on this one.

“It seems like a big one, and all of the team are quite confident. Monza, it’s maybe not the best place to bring upgrades necessarily, because you don’t see the full effect of the benefit, of course, with this track, which is a much more drag-sensitive one than maybe last week was.

“Nonetheless, it’s been a long time coming. The team have worked incredibly hard, and we have a lot of challenges that we face. Being a small team, one of them is the turnaround times of our upgrades, and you’ve seen that. The last big one that we brought was in Canada, which is a long way back. Hopefully it’s going to be a good weekend for us.”

Ocon, who had a few difficult races in the middle of the season, is equally upbeat about the upgrades.

“I'm excited to drive this new car,” said the Frenchman. “Obviously, we have the new aero package. I drove it in the simulator on Tuesday, and yeah, it felt better there. Of course, we need to translate it to the track. It's not always a given that it will perform like that on track.

“But everybody's excited in the office, and looking forward to see what this car can do. And obviously, it's not the most technical circuit for it, so we are not going to see the full gain. We are more going to see that in Madrid. But it will still be interesting to see how the car feels in the Lesmos and Parabolica compared to before. So it is quite a big package, and I'm looking forward to driving it.”

Ocon’s suggestion that it’s a “new car” gives some idea of the scale of the upgrade package, and that’s backed up by the strategy that the team has adopted for the weekend.

In the past it has often conducted back-to-back tests between new and old spec cars on Friday, and then converted the latter for Saturday.

This time both cars are in the new spec from the start of FP1, a reflection of the fact that changing on Friday evening would be a huge job – and likely involve playing a curfew joker.

“Ideally, we want to back-to-back it,” said Team Principal Ayao Komatsu. “But because of the parts involved, it's very difficult to back-to-back, like to combat the car on Friday night, for instance, that was going to be challenging. One to break the curfew, two, in terms of quality of the job we can do.

“Yes, it's nice to actually measure exactly how much performance you put on the car, but at the same time we don't want to risk that Friday night s**t fight. But also, let's face it, if we had a car capable of scoring points at the baseline, we might take a different view.

“But if we don't do anything, we're not going to score points. So we rather put it all in, believe that it's going to work, and then make sure that we do a very good quality preparation.”

As mentioned earlier only Bearman has the new Ferrari power unit this weekend, and why he and not Ocon has the benefit of it is an interesting tale in itself, given that usually Haas try to be as fair as possible across the two cars.

Ferrari is only obliged to provide its customer teams with one upgraded power unit when the works cars get a new spec. In essence given the need to squeeze out everything possible at Monza, Haas did not want to wait until two were available just to be fair to both drivers. Thus the difficult choice was made to give only one car the benefit.

“Last time around we didn't do that,” Komatsu confirmed. “We waited until we had enough engines to introduce to both drivers together. Obviously Monza, as you know, it's a very power-sensitive circuit. So it's a shame to have performance sitting in the garage, right?

“Of course, it makes it very challenging. So yes, it would have been better if two engines are available at least. But again, Ferrari is pushing like hell to get as much performance on the engine as possible. Of course, they want to introduce it at Monza, for the reasons I just said to you. So that means they’ve got minimum quantity, just to satisfy the regulation.”

So why did Bearman get the nod? He’s ahead of Ocon in the World Championship, but that wasn’t the only factor at play.

“Of course, that's part of the consideration,” said Komatsu. “But again, it's not an aerodynamic upgrade, but the last items we had, like the CI [Carbon Industrie] brakes test, Esteban was actually struggling more on brake locking, etcetera. So considering that the Montreal upgrade, we got it on Ollie first, we decided to give that brake upgrade to Esteban first.

“We had another upgrade on the power steering before shutdown in Budapest. Again, we decided to give that to Esteban, because again he was more vocal about it, and he was struggling more on the power steering feel. So the last two upgrades we gave to Esteban – this this time around it's a back to Ollie.”

title: Why Tsunoda feels ‘like a rookie’ for Racing Bulls return
excerpt:
When Yuki Tsunoda was told he would be driving for Racing Bulls at the Dutch Grand Prix, he was on holiday on a beach in Greece and had to rush to prepare for the outing at Zandvoort. He felt so unprepared that he approached the weekend like a rookie.

By the time the Italian Grand Prix came around, Tsunoda had already been working in the simulator in case Isack Hadjar remained sidelined. Despite having a race weekend in the car under his belt and more time to prepare, he still feels like a rookie given the complexity of energy deployment at Monza.

“It was actually yesterday,” Tsunoda said on Thursday when asked when he had learned the news. “I was in the sim just in case. I really didn't know until mid-afternoon, and I heard in the middle of the session. ‘OK, I’m going to drive, so I’ll keep doing the simulator work as I would in a race week.’”

Zandvoort went about as well as could have been expected, given Tsunoda’s unfamiliarity with the car and the demands of a Sprint weekend. After finishing a solid P11, he received positive feedback from Team Principal Alan Permane.

“[It was] positive for sure,” the Japanese racer confirmed. “And even after the debrief, I said, ‘Good luck this season, I enjoyed it,’ or something. Alan said, ‘We might need you again – we might need you again next week. So be prepared.’

“I could tell that I felt some more trust from him after that race. If I did really bad, and anything can happen with this world, maybe I wouldn't get called to drive this week. So yeah, I think this was very positive.”

Although final confirmation came late, Tsunoda had spent the days after Zandvoort assuming he might be needed. He therefore focused on training, working with the Faenza engineers and running in the simulator.

“I was pretty much really chilled, like a usual race week. I was more prepared, I would say, than the week before in the Netherlands, because it all happened suddenly, and now after Isack was injured, I was more prepared.

Lawson to replace Hadjar again at Red Bull in Monza

“So that was probably the healthiest one week I spent in 2026 so far! So yeah, I was really prepared. I'm feeling more ready than ever.”

The biggest challenge now is energy deployment around Monza, an area where Tsunoda lacks the race experience of the drivers who have competed throughout this season, taking in the long straights at places like Shanghai and Spa-Francorchamps.

“I think Netherlands was fortunately one of the easiest tracks I would say to manage the energy, and I can say that I was able to adjust to the car pretty smoothly," said Tsunoda.

“But now it's the most difficult track for that energy deployment, and I already experienced in the simulator how different it is, and really kicks in these challenges of these regulations.

“So yeah, the management, brake early or whatever, those things I really have to practice. And in the simulator, it felt really weird, because I know I can drive faster – but you cannot, because otherwise in total lap time, you'll be slow. So that will be the biggest challenge for me.”

Being quick over a single lap is one thing, but Tsunoda must also adjust to the tactical, energy-management battles that were less prominent at Zandvoort.

“I think it will be more challenging in race condition,” he admitted. “Because this kind of strategic, I would say, battle with the energy management with other cars, I didn't do that, and probably other [drivers] know what the car is going to do after they use the battery to overtake or defend. I only know from the simulator, and the Netherlands was probably the least powerful.

“In short runs I would say I'm not worried as much, because you have free practice anyway, so you know what kind of things, and you can only focus on yourself. But in the race, you have to be proactive, right? So that's the only thing that I have to be more prepared for sure than the Netherlands.”

Tsunoda is hoping to take a step forward from Zandvoort, with a place in Q3 and points on Sunday his ideal scenario. However, he knows it will not be easy.

"I will see for FP1 these energy things, how difficult it is. I really don't know. But I think the car pace is good, and we’re bringing an upgrade here, so I am excited to see that.

“I think the Netherlands was more like I just entered the race a bit like a rookie, so I just tried to learn as much as possible. The time was very tight because of the Sprint format.

“I have to practice a lot of things, like energy deployments, and even over one lap to be patient. I would say I feel like I'm a rookie, and I have to try and learn everything, and try to not miss any single thing that the team is instructing me.”

He also has a special reason to want a good result this weekend: “I want to do well here – I’ve never done well here. Out of five years, I have three DNFs, two I didn't even start. So I don't know what's going on with here, but getting this opportunity, hopefully it’s lucky.”

title: Verstappen sets out target for Monza
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has admitted that he and Red Bull “need to be realistic” about their chances at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix, with the Dutchman setting out the aim of “just trying to have a good weekend”.

Verstappen’s home event last time out in Zandvoort ended in disappointing fashion after he suffered a crash at the end of the first lap, putting him out of the running while stand-in team mate Liam Lawson salvaged points for the squad in P7.

Looking ahead to Monza, Verstappen will sit out Free Practice 1 as Ayumu Iwasa gets behind the wheel before he returns to action for FP2 – and while it is a track that he claimed victory at last season, the four-time World Champion is keeping his expectations modest this time around.

“Let's see,” he said of his prospects. “Of course I'm not doing FP1, so we'll see afterwards how the car will be. Trying to get it into a nice window, but at the same time we also need to be realistic, where we are at the moment as a team and how we're performing.

“We’ll just try to have a good weekend. I know it's already going to be very complex with the energy around here, so we just need to try and understand that first and then we'll just see from there where we are in the pecking order.

“Just going off the last few races, I think we just need to be realistic.”

Looking back at the difficult end to what will be the last Dutch Grand Prix, Verstappen conceded that he does not think it would have been a particularly strong outing even if he had been able to continue.

“I would have loved to have completed the race, even though I don’t think it would have been a magic race for us pace-wise,” he explained.

“The whole weekend we were a bit off, and I was not feeling well so all the combinations were not there.

“But I look back at it with a lot of positives – I won races there, we had really great moments with the fans there, so overall it was a crazy experience and I’m very happy that I got to have a home Grand Prix like that.”

title: Why Piastri wants answers to a ‘bigger question’ in Monza
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes he and McLaren have "got ideas on how we can make things better" ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, after the Australian has struggled for performance in recent races.

Team mate and reigning World Champion Lando Norris has put McLaren back on top in Formula 1 after winning the two previous races in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Although Piastri fought for the win in the former before retiring, he was noticeably lacking pace compared with Norris at Zandvoort, finishing 32 seconds adrift of the race winner.

The Dutch Grand Prix marked a complete year since Piastri stood on the top step of the podium, having watched his lead in last year's drivers' standings eventually surpassed by Norris.

Speaking on Thursday's media day ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, Piastri admitted that his struggles were not due to one reason specifically, making it harder to rectify.

"I think it's never been the same issue or thing we're chasing every weekend. It's always been slightly different which I think kind of raises a bigger question," he said.

"If it was just one thing we kept struggling with it would, in some ways, be a bit of an easy fix but I think the fact we've kind of found different ways of having difficulty, we've been trying to answer that question.

"And we are getting closer, finding more ideas and ultimately the only way you can really solve it is by trying stuff on track. Not saying that we've gone away and found this problem, we've definitely got ideas on how we can make things better, both from how I drive the car and how we set up the car.

"Hopefully we can find something that works a bit better. I think in Zandvoort, Qualifying was a much bigger step, Lando and I were very close but clearly in the race there was a deficit. That's the area we're trying to work on."

Piastri believes that the new-for-2026 regulations have created a breed of car which he has struggled to adapt to, while bad luck and reliability problems have also played their part.

"There's definitely things that have not been as easy or as comfortable this year compared to last year," he said.

"Some things we can fix quickly, some things we can't. I think these cars in general, the concept is very different, the tyres are quite different.

"There's a lot of things as well that are not necessarily in our control. Also this season not been easy for other reasons, we've had a lot of struggles with reliability or bad luck."

title: McLaren hit back at 'insulting' Flavio Briatore allegations
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has hit back at the allegations made by Alpine boss Flavio Briatore, who questioned the impartiality of the hearing process surrounding the Monaco Grand Prix results.

In late August, a panel of four judges heard the arguments of those involved as McLaren and Red Bull sought to have Pierre Gasly's five-second time penalty for pit lane speeding reimposed.

Gasly crossed the line in third place but was dropped to seventh, before Alpine successfully overturned the penalty as it cited a concern around the timing loops in the Monaco pit lane.

However, McLaren and Red Bull lodged their protest, creating a process that lasted several months before the ruling was finally made this week.

But in a spectacular accusation, Briatore took issue with one judge on the panel - Mr Filippo Marchino - claiming that he was “nasty” and has ties to McLaren through the McLaren Special Operations division.

Stella, however, is far from impressed with the allegations that the judge ruled with a bias toward McLaren.

“I find that this conference, going in this direction, is quite insulting for McLaren,” Stella told media including RacingNews365.

“For the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect and if anybody makes those kind of allegations, which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

“The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this phase like it's been done.”

The decision reinstated Red Bull's Isack Hadjar to the podium, while Oscar Piastri found himself boosted up to fourth place for the Woking-based squad.

While the ruling offered a points boost for McLaren, Stella insisted the decision was important to offer F1 a sense of clarity.

“It's a decision that we definitely welcome,” he said. “It's important because, first of all, it adds clarity in relation to the application of Article 1.1.1 of the International Sporting Code which is foundational.

“It's foundational for anything that derives from there. We appealed because we wanted to make sure that this clarity was sought.

“We had concerns which were beyond the fact that we might have lost two championship points. We were concerned about the application of sporting quality and fairness, and this is important.

“This is not only important for McLaren. In fact, not only Red Bull, but all teams were present in the hearing because this was a very important moment, in terms of clarification as to how we apply the rules, as to how we apply consistency.

“Also in the specific case, consistency is related to the methodologies that are valid throughout our race weekend.”

title: Flavio Briatore accuses FIA judge of 'McLaren bias' in extraordinary claims
excerpt:
Alpine boss Flavio Briatore has accused a judge on the FIA's International Court of Appeal hearing of being biased against the team amid purported links to McLaren.

On Friday, the ruling of the International Court of Appeal was handed down, with the panel deciding to reinstate the two five-second time penalties originally handed to Alpine's Pierre Gasly for speeding in the pit-lane.

Gasly had finished third on the road, but dropped to seventh in the final results once the penalties had been added to his elapsed race time, but Alpine successfully lodged a right of review to overturn the penalties after it was found the official timekeeper had made a mistake in measuring the length of the pit lane.

McLaren and Red Bull, whose Isack Hadjar was promoted to third, stripped of it, and then reinstated after Friday's ruling, lodged the hearing with the FIA's International Court of Appeal, which was heard in September.

Shortly after the verdict was announced, in the FIA's Team Principal's Press Conference, Briatore launched his astonishing claims at one of the four panel members.

"Sorry, this is very unfair," Briatore began to media, including RacingNews365.

"First, we accept the decision, but what is very strange is of the four judges on the panel, one of the judges acts like a prosecutor.

"For us, that's not a big problem. The problem is that he's very linked with McLaren, because we have a nice picture of this guy at the speech for McLaren in 2018 at McLaren Special Operations (MSO) in Beverly Hills.

"He has a foundation called One Drop Foundation, and McLaren gave a car. This is quite unfair. One of the judges was linked with a team protesting us."

After McLaren boss Andrea Stella attempted to make a defence of the team's decision to appeal on the basis of sporting integrity, Briatore dismissed this.

"What is unfair is that the judge was linked with McLaren; this is unfair. The judge normally needs to be completely independent, and this judge was very nasty during the hearing. He was acting as a prosecutor, and after, we found out why the reason was he so nasty. The guy is very linked with McLaren.

"Whatever Stella says for the sport, first I think about the judgement is that you have to be independent, and doing a speech for McLaren, and somebody using McLaren cars in the charity- this is the point.

"After that, points 1.1.2,3,4,5 [of the rules], I don't care; I'm very surprised this guy has been dealing with McLaren.

"We had no idea this guy was linked with McLaren. We went to the hearing with McLaren, and we saw it was very funny because this judge was not a judge; he was a prosecutor. Afterwards, we found out this guy was linked with the McLaren team; this is what I think. So it's quite unfair if some of the judge is one of the team fighting with us.

"The decision in Monaco was from the same people, because the stewards talking about are the same. Everything was done the same, and I accept everything. What I do not accept is when you have the judge, the panel. We need somebody independent.

"Our big question is this: Why was somebody involved with McLaren part of the panel in the in this case?

"We accept the result of the hearing. What was very disappointing is to find out that one of the judges has a very good relationship with McLaren, a working relationship, kind.

"The panel should be completely independent, and you don't need somebody linked with some team, especially the team involved with us in this situation. Only that. Nothing. Now we see. We think about what we can do next."

title: F1 announce spectacular launch event ahead of 2027 season
excerpt:
F1 has announced that it will host a season launch event once again in 2027, building on the showcase it put on in 2025.

Last year, the campaign kicked off with a one-night event at the O2 Arena in London, where all of the teams unveiled their cars for the year ahead.

The drivers and team principals were present, with the launch streamed live on YouTube for fans to tune in.

In a major change to the idea, next year's occasion will take place across three days, from February 18-20 in Milan.

F1 has detailed that a 'fan festival' will occur on all days, while the main event - labelled F1 The Show - will be on February 18.

F1 added that further details about the event will be announced in the coming months, with tickets going on sale later in the year.

“We are always thinking big and pushing boundaries, and F1 Live Milan is going to be an incredible experience created with our fans at its heart,” said F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali.

“We want them to feel that they are not simply watching the sport, but they are truly immersed in it. It is an important part of our ongoing ambition to bring Formula 1 closer to fans than ever before, giving them the chance to see their heroes up close and experience the energy, innovation, and emotion that make Formula 1 so unique.

“As F1 continues to reach new audiences around the world, racing will always be our soul - but we also want to create unforgettable experiences that bring the excitement of Formula 1 to life on an even bigger scale and continue to explore what is possible.

“Building on the extraordinary success of F1 75 in London, F1 Live Milan will transform the city into a Formula 1 festival for three unforgettable days, bringing people together from across the globe to celebrate everything they love about our sport.

“I know my fellow Italians will offer a fantastic welcome to fans travelling to F1 Live Milan and I cannot wait to see the city come to life with Formula 1 energy, creating memories that will last a lifetime.”

title: Red Bull react to Isack Hadjar Monaco GP podium reinstatement
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has expressed his happiness at Isack Hadjar having his Monaco Grand Prix podium finish returned after Pierre Gasly's time penalties were reimposed.

Originally, the Alpine driver, who crossed the line third in Monte Carlo, took two five-second time penalties at the chequered flag for speeding in the pit lane, which dropped him to seventh.

However, Team Enstone lodged a Right of Review into the results, with that subsequently establishing that those punishments were in error, and Gasly returned to his finishing position on the road.

The problem with that outcome was that multiple drivers, including Oscar Piastri, who finished fifth behind Hadjar, had already served their own penalties for the same issue.

In response to the altered results, Red Bull and McLaren protested the verdict of Alpine's Right of Review, which is what has caused the results to change again, with the initial classification now adopted.

Following confirmation from the FIA Court of Appeals, Mekies responded to the development, which came as FP1 at the Italian Grand Prix got underway.

"Look, first of all, very happy that the court reinstated Isack's podium," the Frenchman told Sky Sports F1.

Not only was the boss of the Milton Keynes-based squad pleased for his driver, but he was also keen to stress the virtue that the outcome has for F1.

"It's important for Isack, but we also did it because we felt it was important for the sport — we don't really think we want to go racing and have to worry after the race about whether the speed limit check is correct or not correct," he added.

"We felt that a lot of cars have complied with the regulations in Monaco on the speed limit, and some cars were overspeeding. Some of them served the penalty; some of them didn't. And it was important that we have a consistent way to go racing.

"So we are happy with the result of the court. It's the very reason why we took it to the [FIA] Court of Appeal. It's because we felt it was important for the sport and, of course, for Isack — it was his first podium with us."

title: FIA release statement after significant Monaco GP podium verdict
excerpt:
The FIA has issued a statement after a final ruling was made on the outcome of the Monaco Grand Prix.

In the hours after the race in early June, Alpine lodged a protest over the two five-second time penalties that were issued to Pierre Gasly.

Due to a timing loop anomaly at the entrance to the pit lane, several drivers were handed five-second time penalties during the race.

However, as Gasly was the only driver not to serve his punishment during the event, Alpine had scope to lodge an appeal after the grand prix.

The stewards ruled in his favour and reinstated him to third, much to the dismay of McLaren and Red Bull, who lodged a protest of their own, which was heard in late August.

It was then determined that Gasly's penalties should be reimposed, demoting him once again to seventh in the order.

The FIA itself insisted that the evidence presented to the stewards and that given in court differ greatly due to the major legal involvement of the latter.

Nevertheless, the sport's governing body vowed to use the situation to further streamline its own practices going forward.

“The FIA is reviewing the methodology and operation of the current Formula 1 timing system and the related regulatory matters,” a statement from the governing body read.

“It will also be reviewing other judicial procedures and operations including the right of review and the appeal processes.

“The FIA is fully supportive of the Stewarding process and the independence and objectivity of the diverse panels of Stewards who are an integral part of global motorsport.

“Stewards’ decisions are taken in a different environment to that of the Court, whereas the Court has access to extensive and additional legal counsel input, arguments and evidence.

“The FIA Stewards constantly review their processes and take part in extensive professional development.

“Every decision of the ICA is carefully examined by FIA Stewards ensuring a process of continuous improvement."

title: Alpine take firm stance after Monaco GP podium decision: 'Unjustly punished'
excerpt:
The Alpine F1 team has released a statement following the ruling over the outcome of the Monaco Grand Prix podium.

In June, Pierre Gasly crossed the line in third place but dropped down the order at the chequered flag after being deemed to have sped in the pit lane during the race.

He was one of several drivers to fall foul of the rule, but as his penalty was not served in the race, Alpine appealed the punishment. The FIA ruled in its favour, with the situation complicated by the positioning of timing loops that measure the average speed.

However, McLaren and Red Bull then opposed the decision, and a hearing was held on August 25 in Paris to settle the matter.

In its decision, the FIA International Court determined that the penalties on Gasly should be reimposed, dropping him back to seventh place and reinstating Isack Hadjar to the podium.

Alpine has questioned the nature of the findings, feeling it was unfairly stripped from the podium.

“The team expresses its disappointment and frustration with the outcome reached by the FIA International Court of Appeal relating to the result of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix,” read a statement from Alpine.

“While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that Car #10 did not exceed the Pit Lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

“While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive Championship fight.

“This outcome will not deter the team’s efforts and motivation in achieving its objectives by the end of the season.”
